s: Go AI – Designing shopping without the shopping.
I led design on an AI platform that shops for you, reaching 15% adoption and 28% higher order value across 50M+ users in 4 weeks.
A three-way partnership between Gopuff, SpaceX AI, and Eight Inc., spanning product, design, AI, and engineering.
Gopuff and SpaceX AI set out to build something that didn't exist yet: a grocery platform that shops for you.
Go predicts what you're running low on, builds baskets for you around real moments in your life, and delivers in under 15 minutes.
I led the design across the full Go experience.
Together with the Eight inc team, I was responsible for the interaction design, the Moments system, the AI's visual language, and the brand expression that would carry it.
My job was translating an enormously ambitious AI capability into something people would actually trust with their groceries.
We shipped it.
Then the data told us which parts were working and which weren't, and that's where the real design challenge started.
The early direction was minimal and it was fractured.
The initial brief was to add an intelligent chatbot AI model that could help users with their shopping.
I didn't want to build just another chatbot experience; instead I took the opportunity to design something that felt revolutionary, industry changing and never seen before.
A product that shops for you.
It predicts what you want thanks to the access Gopuff has to a scale of data no one else does.
The first design approach was clean.
White screens, simple typography, a pared-back interface that tried to get out of the way.
The logic made sense on paper: reduce friction, reduce noise, let the AI do the work.But something wasn't landing.
The more we stripped back, the more the product felt like any other grocery app.
We had a three-tab system: Ask, Explore, and Go Bag.
Each did something distinct and each did it reasonably well in isolation.
Together they broke the product.
Users didn't know where to start.
They didn't know where to go next.
They'd land in Ask, not know what to say, tab over to Explore, lose the thread, and never reach the bag we'd built for them.
We tried to solve it with onboarding.
It didn't work, and that's usually the tell.
When onboarding is doing the work your information architecture should be doing, the architecture is wrong.
The minimal visual direction added more weight to it and made it worse.
Stripping the interface back removed the very signals users needed to orient themselves.
The AI's intelligence had nowhere to live.
There was no way to look at a screen and sense that anything remarkable was happening underneath it.
The constraint wasn't technical.
It was structural and creative.
And I'd been trying to fix it with refinements when the whole shape was wrong.
I flew to Miami and ran a two-day whiteboard and rapid prototyping workshop with the CEOs and the full Gopuff and SpaceX AI teams.
I led the sessions, and I set myself a hard condition going in: I wasn't flying back to London without a direction the entire room was genuinely proud of.
The visual direction went the opposite way from minimal: hyper-real, immersive product photography set in actual environments.
Groceries laid out on your kitchen table.
The BBQ you'll be having in 15 minutes.
Not a product-led experience, but a moment-driven one showing you what you're about to live once the delivery arrives.
We collapsed everything into a single page.The input field is the entry point to the conversation with Go.
No tab, no navigation, just type or speak.
The first thing users see is the auto-added predicted Moment: a bag Go has already built for you, ready to go.
Swiping up moves you to the next Moment, and the next, TikTok-style, a vertical feed of AI-generated baskets to discover, explore, and get inspired by.
Weeks of prior work, gone.
I wasn't precious about it.
The cost of shipping the wrong structure was far higher than the cost of restarting.
Chat, prediction, and discovery collapsed into one page with a vertical Moment feed.
The three-tab system's core failure was making users navigate to find value.
The new model delivers value first and makes navigation optional.
The Go wordmark became a glowing light source, appearing wherever the AI is thinking or speaking.
Users learn fast: when it's glowing, Go is working.
A trust cue built into the identity rather than explained in copy.

gopuff.h: Shop by Moments. Baskets built around real life
s: BBQ Day, Game Day, a 5am gym session, Puppy Treat Day.
Each with a specific reason attached; "Your usual post-basketball recovery, with extra electrolytes.
It's hot out today." Being specific is what makes an AI recommendation feel trustworthy rather than arbitrary.
Every item editable (quantity, swap, remove) alongside "Add all" for users who want to accept a Moment in one tap.
The goal was partial acceptance: keep what's right, change what isn't, never feel forced into all-or-nothing.
We shipped an MVP to 4,000 users and tested not just the prediction engine, but everything around it.
Did the UX hold up without a facilitator in the room?
Was the tone of voice landing?
Did the copy read as helpful or presumptuous?
Was the brand implementation coherent across every surface a user could hit?
After a few quick corrections and iterations, promising early metrics gave us the confidence to go wide.
We launched publicly to 50+ million users across the US.
Adoption at real scale.
Go reached a 15% usage rate across tens of thousands of daily visits, roughly one in seven eligible users choosing it organically, inside an established app where people already had a shopping habit.
Go users spent 28% more per order.
That's the number I'm proudest of.
It reframes Go from a convenience feature into a commercial driver: people who used it didn't just shop differently, they shopped bigger.
Growing 8.2% week on week, with Go's share of total Gopuff product revenue up 12.5% WoW.
Around 2,720 Go orders per day, with nearly one in three ordering visits producing a Go-attributed order.
Public launch was the start of the design process, not the end.
I worked directly from the Go performance dashboards, and the week-on-week movement is where the real story is.
Explore revenue grew 73.2% week on week.
Explore became the fastest-growing part of Go.
That's the clearest evidence I have that scrapping the three-tab model was right, and it's what I'd point to if anyone asked whether the lost weeks were worth it.
Conversion rose 21.1% WoW to 14.6%.
More users completing purchases each week as the experience got clearer.
Full bag removal fell 8.8% WoW to 46%.
Early on, a large share of users were deleting Go's entire suggested basket.
A blunt signal they didn't trust it yet.
The problem wasn't the concept, it was the details: wrong quantities, wrong brands, too many items.
Making those easy to swap moved users from rejecting everything to keeping part of it, which was exactly the shift I'd designed for.
Revenue per bag rose 15.5% WoW to $3.90.
Every basket a user saw was worth more than the week before, not because we showed more, but because the ones we showed were better matched and easily editable.

gopuff.h: The insight that changed the product again
s: Reading the behaviour data, one pattern jumped out: a large share of users were using chat as a search bar.
Typing "milk." Typing "ramen." Searching instead of taking advantage of the SpaceX AI model capabilities to recommend the right set of products.
At first this was treated as a failure of the “Ask Me Anything” education, and partly it was.
But the more honest read was that it was a very common behaviour we hadn't designed for.
Sometimes shoppers want inspiration.
Sometimes they know exactly what they need and want it in their bag in ten seconds.
We'd built beautifully for the first case and left the second one behind a chat window.
So I improved the education around how to talk to Go, making the conversational capability discoverable rather than assumed.

I also made it far easier to browse and explore categories inside and outside the chat experience, with the same imagery and recommendation logic running through it, so it never felt like a bolted-on fallback.

I designed toward creating the user's personal “Aisle”: somewhere they come back to and know exactly where everything is, like their local supermarket, for the times they don't want inspiration and just want utility.
Average items added to cart went from 7 to 11.
That's a 57% increase, and it came from reading behaviour honestly rather than defending the original design intent.
Onboarding can't fix architecture – If users need to be taught where to go, the structure is wrong.
Collapsing three tabs into one surface did more for comprehension than any amount of tutorial ever did.
Knowing when to restart – Refinement has a ceiling.
Recognising you've hit it is harder and more valuable than iterating toward the wrong answer.
Locking a room for two days until we found a direction everyone believed in was the highest-leverage thing I did on this project.
Design for the behaviour you observe, not the one you intended – Users treating chat as search wasn't them using it wrong.
It was a mode we hadn't served.
Serving it took average cart size from 7 items to 11.
Read the trend, not the snapshot – A 46% full-bag removal rate looks alarming in isolation.
Down 8.8% WoW and still falling, it's a product earning trust in real time.
The product that shipped didn't exist when I started.
What I'm most proud of isn't a screen.

It's the decision to collapse a structure that wasn't working, the two days in Miami spent holding a room until we had something worth building, and then the discipline to keep designing against real behaviour once 50 million people had access to it.
Go proved that people will let AI shop for them, but only if the interface earns their trust.
And earning it is a design challenge, not an LLM one.
I led the redesign of the creator, turning a fragmented flow into a seamless journey boosting game completion rates by over 3×.
Upit represents the future of game development.
A platform where anyone can create games through natural conversation with an AI assistant named Ava.
As the gaming industry becomes more accessible, the challenge was to close the gap between powerful creation capabilities and user-friendly design.

The creator side of Upit needed a complete UX/UI redesign to support the platform's vision: enabling game creation through AI assistance while maintaining the depth and functionality that creators need.
This case study explores the collaborative redesign of the creator experience, driven by a multidisciplinary team of engineers, project managers, stakeholders, and creators.
I developed the project from concept to a refined interface, making AI-powered game development approachable for creators at every level.
Creating games traditionally requires specialised skills in coding, art, design, and sound, which most people do not possess.
Even existing "accessible" platforms like Roblox still require significant technical expertise.
Even for those with some technical ability, the process is notoriously time-consuming, frustrating, and often leads to projects being abandoned.
Make AI assistance feel natural rather than robotic or limiting.

As Senior Product Designer, I led the complete redesign of Upit's creator platform, working closely with the product team, engineering, and stakeholders to reimagine how creators interact with AI-powered game development tools.
Mapping the end‑to‑end flow, from ideation through asset editing, code updates and publishing, and identifying friction points.
Translating complex AI capabilities into intuitive user interactions.
Creating high‑fidelity prototypes and visual designs for web and mobile, then conducting user tests and design reviews with stakeholders.
Collaborating with engineers to align the design system with the platform’s technical requirements.
I planned the user interface and interaction flows across various platforms, prioritising a "mobile-first" approach.
This included the editor's layout, core chat functionality with features like live code preview, and AI-powered tools for image editing and sound editing.
I mapped key flows for AI chat prompts, image generation, code editing, and previewing.
The new navigation grouped related actions, ensuring creators would never feel lost.
Collaborated closely with engineering to build a scalable architecture, focusing on clear planning for iterative development.
This included defining achievable MVPs and mapping out phased rollouts to ensure steady progress.

Designed systems to drive user retention, such as social connections and progress mechanics, as well as features supporting the creator economy like in-app purchases, revenue sharing, and future subscription models.

Developed new interaction patterns specifically for AI-powered creation tools, including conversational UI architecture, mixed initiative patterns (balancing user control with proactive AI assistance), and multimodal interactions.
This required unique approaches beyond traditional UX methodologies to create natural human-AI collaboration.
I implemented a testing workflow combining moderated usability testing, A/B testing and behavioural analytics.
This data-driven approach included design reviews, user testing, and continuous performance monitoring to ensure designs met both user needs and business objectives.
To validate our assumptions and goals, I conducted competitive analyses and user interviews.
Competitor insights: I looked at Roblox, Unity and other game‑creation platforms.
These tools are powerful but require substantial learning and offer little community engagement.
The old editor either demanded significant technical expertise.
This gap informed my focus on conversation‑driven creation.
Target user interviews: I spoke with hobbyist game creators and players.
Many identified themselves as “generalists” who understood high‑level concepts but felt overwhelmed by coding and asset pipelines.
They wanted the AI to scaffold the technical work while giving them the freedom to iterate on ideas.
The redesign was tested through internal testing sessions and an external beta with 50+ creators.
Key metrics included:
Time to first playable game.
Actions required to publish.
Task success rate for non‑technical users.
Number of games created per tester.
~45 min (average).
≈20 clicks across separate pages.
40 % could complete.
6 steps in one flow.
+66 % (AI handles code and assets).
New design (beta).
−70 % (streamlined navigation).
40 % could complete without help.

Testers reported that the conversational interface reduced anxiety around coding.
Many said that seeing the code being generated in real time made them feel “in control” and offered educational value.
On mobile, the compact navigation and simplified asset editor received positive feedback for being intuitive and touch‑friendly.
The new journey begins with a full‑screen “Ask Ava” screen, where users simply describe the game they want to build.
A friendly illustration and explanatory text communicate that Ava is their AI companion.
This reduces the intimidation factor and sets the tone for a playful creation process.
Once the user submits a prompt, Ava generates a game design document and starts streaming the source code, assets and sounds.
The chat interface shows progress indicators and options to stop or adjust generation.
The AI’s responses are written as if a designer were explaining their decisions, making the process feel collaborative.
Testers appreciated the clear progress feedback and the ability to intervene if the result wasn’t what they expected.
Designing the creator side of Upit reinforced several takeaways:
Guided conversation approach – By allowing users to speak to Ava as they would to a collaborator, we lowered the learning curve and increased engagement.
Focus on casual gamers – Empowering these users meant prioritising simplicity over power.
I deliberately limited advanced features to keep the interface approachable while leaving room for future expert tools.
Cross‑functional collaboration – This redesign involved close collaboration between design, engineering and AI researchers.
Aligning on technical constraints early prevented rework and ensured a polished experience.
Metrics drive iteration – Tracking quantitative metrics like time to create a game and task success rate informed design decisions.
Qualitative feedback from the beta brought many refinements such as adding progress indicators and simplifying navigation.

By turning the complex process of coding into a guided conversation, Upit enables more people to bring their ideas to life fulfilling the company’s vision of empowering everyone to create, play and build communities through games.
As a lead designer, I drove key product improvements that significantly increased user engagement and retention.
Upit is a social platform where players can discover indie games and creators can build new titles with the help of AI.
The redesign of Upit's Play Screen represents a strong and fundamental evolution in balancing gaming mechanics and social elements.

Through iterative design and A/B testing, I led the transformation of the Play Screen from a purely functional interface to a socially-engaged gaming experience that increased average daily social interactions by up to 95% while maintaining core gaming metrics.
User research and analytics revealed several pain points with the original experience.
Low engagement and retention.
First‑day retention for players was about 16–17 % and even lower for creators (≈ 14 %), while average daily social interactions (ADSI) were only 0.142.
Players typically closed the game after a round instead of exploring communities or creators.
Lack of recognition for creators.
Upit’s product vision emphasises core social needs such as validation, community connection, learning and audience building.
The old play screen did not encourage players to follow, comment on or remix games.
Many players did not realise they could join communities, follow developers or remix games.
Users rarely explored beyond the single title they were playing.
The challenge was to introduce social features that would enhance rather than detract from the core gaming experience.
I joined Upit as a Senior Product Designer to lead the full redesign of the play experience across mobile and desktop.
My role covered the entire process, from defining the problem to delivering polished designs.
Key responsibilities included:
Collaborating closely with engineers, product managers, and stakeholders.
Using research and data to identify challenges and set success metrics.
Understanding technical constraints and iterating quickly with engineers.
Leading design exploration, wireframing, prototyping, and visual design for the play screen and its components.
Working with the growth team to design and analyse A/B tests to validate assumptions.
From these insights I defined a set of goals for the new play screen:
Show clearer information about the game’s author, allow players to follow them and show status markers (e.g. medals, achievements) to build trust.
Make it easy to comment, vote, share and join communities.
Integrate these actions into the paused states rather than hiding them on separate pages.
Provide clear entry points to remix a game or apply to become a creator, aligning with our product goal of turning players into creators.
Create reasons for users to return beyond just playing games such as saving games progress, leaderboards and daily challenges with other players.
Add social features ensuring social features don't negatively impact gaming metrics such as rounds started, session duration and unique games played.
I analysed internal data and interviewed both players and creators.
The interviews revealed strong motivations: creators wanted recognition and validation, and players enjoyed community connection and challenges (collecting achievements or medals).
I conducted competitive analysis of platforms like TikTok, Roblox and itch.io, showing how social feedback loops (likes, comments, remixes) drive retention.
I also analysed the old play experience and mapped out the user journey from finishing a round to leaving the app noticing that the drop‑off after the game‑over screen was steep.
I sketched multiple concepts that combined gameplay with social features.
Early wireframes explored modular overlays that could appear at the end of a round: a score summary, quick‑action buttons, a comment feed and a section for remixes.
I then built interactive Figma prototypes and ran usability tests with five players and five creators.
Players appreciated immediate recognition and the visually appealing banners and icons but were overwhelmed when too many elements appeared at once.
Moreover, comments and upvotes needed to be visible in context, burying them behind a tab clearly reduced interaction.

Throughout the design and implementation of the play screen, I worked closely with a diverse, multidisciplinary team, including engineers, designers, and data analysts, to refine the new layouts in response to component limitations prioritising user retention, social engagement and accessibility.
Together, we established a comprehensive design system with reusable components for cards, buttons, banners, and lists, which supported rapid iteration and effective cross-functional collaboration.
We validated the new play screen through two large A/B tests.
Our first A/B test compared the new design (V2) with the existing play screen for a total of two consecutive weeks.
The test targeted both desktop and mobile users in a 50/50 split.
ADSI – social interactions.
Game session duration.
Unique games played.
V2 change vs.
The new design dramatically increased social activity, particularly on desktop: comments per daily active user rose by 240%, and communities joined increased by 40%.
However, the added friction and animation-heavy transitions reduced game engagement, especially on mobile: session duration fell by 22% on mobile and rounds started dropped by 33%.
Retention was slightly worse for registered users, suggesting that we needed to balance social interaction with core gameplay.
In response to these trade‑offs we iterated on the design.
We reduced animation times, simplified buttons, removed visual clutter and added quicker ways to restart a round.
A second A/B test (V2.1) ran with the same 50/50 split.
V2.1 change vs.
This iteration successfully retained the social gains while mitigating many gaming losses.
D1 retention equalised across platforms and ADSI almost doubled on desktop.
Mobile still showed declines in rounds started and unique games played, but the drops were smaller than in V2.
Based on these results we rolled out V2.1 to 100 % of users while planning further optimisations for mobile.
To further enhance user experience and drive engagement, I closely analysed feedback and performance data from earlier versions of the play screen.
Between V2 and V2.1 I made several notable changes.
The most impactful results:
I reduced the transitions between play rounds from 2–3 seconds to under 1 second, which helped increase rounds started by 14 % on desktop.
The score banner was reduced in size with a simpler and cleaner visual design.
The Play again button was emphasised and made the main CTA.
Secondary actions (upvote, share, more) were moved to a compact row, reducing clutter.
Instead of automatically showing a full feed, comments now appear in an expandable sheet.
Players can quickly scan a few comments and leave one without scrolling away from the play controls.
Balance is critical - Adding social layers boosted engagement but initially hurt core gameplay.
Iterative design via A/B testing helped find a sweet spot where social actions enhanced the play experience.
Mobile is not desktop - The same design can have huge different effects across devices.
Mobile players are very sensitive to latency and clutter; small changes in animation and layout can have a great impact on key metrics.
Analyse everything - Without comprehensive analytics we would not have detected the decline in session duration or the recovery after adjustments.
Partnering with data analysts early on was essential.

This project demonstrates how a comprehensive, data‑driven design process can transform a seemingly simple screen into a social hub that celebrates creators and builds community while keeping the solid structure of the gameplay experience.
Led product design and UX, delivering an accessible AI-powered platform for collectors.
Hero is a platform designed to revolutionize the collectibles market by combining an innovative marketplace with customizable spaces to display collections.
We’ve built a system where collectors can buy, sell, and showcase their items while benefiting from cutting-edge AI technology.

Hero’s AI-driven features provide seamless authentication of collectibles and accurate price predictions, helping collectors understand the true value of their items and anticipate future market trends.
Auction houses charge up to 35% in fees, and platforms like eBay are saturated with fake items, making transactions risky and expensive.
Verifying collectibles traditionally requires expert evaluation, which is neither scalable nor efficient.
Determining the true market value of collectibles is often a lengthy and imprecise process, adding frustration for both buyers and sellers.
Hero addresses these pain points with an innovative approach.
Both buyers and sellers are fully ID-verified, with payments held in escrow to guarantee security.
A proprietary AI model is designed to authenticate collectibles, eliminating the need for physical expert verification.
The AI system not only provides accurate valuations based on current data but also predicts future values, offering collectors a deeper insight into the market trends.
As the Product Designer and Project Manager, I played a central role in shaping the entire visual identity and user experience of Hero.
I led the User Experience Design by mapping end to end user journeys and defining detailed task flows for core actions such as onboarding, bidding, authentication, and valuation.
These flows were built from real behavioural insights and helped align product, design, and engineering around a shared understanding of user intent, friction points, and success states.
I conducted generative user research through interviews and usability sessions with active collectors to uncover motivations, trust barriers, and decision making patterns across buying and selling.
These insights directly informed information architecture, interaction design, and prioritisation of features.
I ran iterative usability testing across low fidelity wireframes and high fidelity prototypes, validating assumptions, stress testing critical flows, and refining edge cases before development.
Feedback from each testing round was translated into measurable UX improvements that reduced drop offs, increased task completion confidence, and strengthened overall trust in the platform.
I began by mapping out user journeys, flows, and task flows to better understand the customer experience.
We developed low-fidelity wireframes and interactive prototypes to test the initial user experience.
Collectors participated in usability testing and interviews, providing crucial feedback to refine the design.
I worked alongside engineers to design and launch the MVP.
I collaborated closely with engineers ensuring technical feasibility and maintaining a high standard of quality throughout the development process.
This allowed us to begin gathering pricing data, which was essential to training the AI's predictive pricing engine.
The MVP focused on essential functionality, whereas the full launch included AI for authentication and valuation prediction.
Continuous user feedback shaped the development process.
For instance, we discovered that auctions without a reserve price increased item sale percentages, with a 93% higher final sale value compared to those with reserve prices.
I designed an intuitive, user-friendly bidding interface that provides collectors with a seamless experience.
The scrollable wheel encourages higher participation by making bid placement easy and engaging, which in turn drives up final prices as users are more inclined to place bids effortlessly.
To prevent accidental bids and provide clarity on the final auction cost, we implemented a two-step confirmation process with a bid preview.

This feature addresses user concerns about mistakenly placing bids and offers a transparent view of all relevant details before confirming a bid, informed by insights gathered from user interviews and feedback.
Instead of a traditional countdown timer, we created a dynamic, colour-based timeline that animates as the auction progresses.
This visually engaging feature allows users to quickly grasp how much time is left in the auction.
Additionally, users can view bid history directly along the progress bar, making the auction experience more interactive and engaging, even without an auctioneer.
Drawing inspiration from SoundCloud’s comment player, the scrollable bid history offers users a clear, chronological view of previous bids.
This feature is not only functional but enjoyable to use, enhanced by haptic feedback on mobile devices, making the bidding process both practical and fun.
Designing Hero meant carefully balancing trust, transparency, and incentives.
By making the experience simple and predictable, I reduced friction and increased both the quality and consistency of the data without reducing user confidence.
Hero showed how a marketplace and an AI product can strengthen each other when they are designed together.
As the model improved, the experience became safer and more personal which encouraged more users to take part and generate better data.
This loop is the base for Hero’s next phase as a fully AI powered ecosystem where users can authenticate, value, and track their collections with growing accuracy over time.

The authentication of collectibles remains a major challenge, but our experience with Hero demonstrates that AI can revolutionise this process, making it faster, more accurate, and more scalable than traditional expert evaluation.

The data captured from user interactions on the platform such as transaction history, images, and market behaviour will be instrumental in training and developing the AI models that power Hero’s key features.
The auction system was strategically designed not only to drive user engagement but also to facilitate the collection of critical data necessary to train the AI.

This data will form the foundation for Hero’s future AI-powered features, transforming the platform into a comprehensive tool for collectors to authenticate, value, and understand the trends of their collections.
Drove user-centred design from concept to launch, delivering measurable growth in engagement and daily usage.
Connectible is the world's first social media app for collectors and offers the ability to share, connect, and trade any collectibles they love.
The goal is to connect communities together, by enabling collectors to pursue their passion.
As a Senior Product Designer at Connectible, my primary responsibility was to lead the UX design process for the platform.
This role required a deep involvement in every stage of the design, from conceptualisation to implementation, while also playing a key role in project management.

Collaborating closely with our CTO (previously with Depop), CMO (from Flo Health, with prior experience at Nextdoor and Depop), and our engineering team, I focused on integrating user feedback at every step.
This commitment to a user-centered design approach was crucial in refining and adapting our platform to meet and exceed user expectations.
The success of this methodology is evident in the robust user base we've built, demonstrating the effectiveness of my design strategy in creating a product that resonates with Collectors.
The world of collectors lacked a platform that was both simple and enjoyable for connecting and socialising with each other.
There was a void in the market for collectors seeking validation for their tastes.
Connectible was born out of this necessity.
The design of Connectible as a niche multi-community social platform was driven by insights gathered from user research and interviews.

Informed by valuable feedback and research, it became evident that, for collectors, the act of sharing and receiving validation for their collectibles is as important as the ownership of the collectibles themselves.
This understanding helped me consolidate the design of the MVP.
Create an easy-to-use platform where collectors can connect in dedicated, gated communities.
Encourage collectors to react to and rate each other’s collectibles.
Level the playing field and give trading power back to the collectors by eliminating the need for middlemen.
My design process began with a deep dive into market and user research.
I focused my efforts on Original Comic Art, a niche with approximately 100,000 collectors worldwide.
Connectible primary competitor is an outdated forum-style gallery website (CAF), which presented the business with the challenge of the cold-start problem.
I conducted user research on how to use growth hacks to get a big portion of CAF users before Connectible launch.
The results of this research led me to the conclusion that collectors were not interested in a new and better version of CAF.
On the other hand, they were excited to explore a mobile friendly, easy to use app to chat with collectors, scan their art and share it with new communities.
To understand how collectors behave and interact, I conducted extensive user research.
Collectors often socialise at comic-cons in real life, but they also use digital platforms like CAF for portfolio display, Facebook, Messenger, and Telegram groups for interaction and engagement.
This insight helped us shape the mechanics and usability of our platform, focusing on a human-centered design approach.
How important is interacting with posts?
Collectors that think that interacting with posts and reply to discussions is as important as collecting itself.
Collectors that collect more than 1 collectible.
Users want to see latest uploads on Home Feed.
Users that prefer interacting instead of browsing.
I applied the Jobs Theory to my design thinking, as documented in Clayton M.
Christensen’s “Competing Against Luck,” to understand why customers choose certain products over others.
I viewed this job as a mini-documentary about our consumer’s journey to share their collection and gain validation for what they own.
In-depth interviews with consumers and non-consumers helped me identify the goals, struggles, and obstacles that collectors face.
Daily active users.
Through a iterative design approach, the improvements resulted in a monthly increase of 67% in user interactions.
The integration of new features, such as "comment previews" and "replies to comments", led to collectors sending an impressive 1.5 additional comments and messages daily.
We also had a surge in daily active users by 88% when the user started getting in-app notifications and toasts alerts every time they were engaging with each other.
The design focus is shifting towards "clubs" and small niche groups.

I aim to highlight the discussion-style area over the "latest-uploads feed" and encourage users to create discussions instead of merely showcasing their collections without interacting with each other.
I perfected reactions for comments and replies in threads to comments allowing users to make the most out of discussions.
This iterative process, driven by user feedback, has been instrumental in shaping Connectible into the platform it is today.

Connectible has taught me the pivotal lesson that even users with obsessive personalities won't adopt a platform unless it fulfils a specific job for them, prompting them to "hire" the product and discontinue usage of alternatives.
Shaped the strategy and design to align FRVR's mission with a compelling new digital presence.
FRVR is a next-generation social gaming platform empowering users to both play and co-create games through AI-driven tools.
As Senior Product Designer, I was tasked with designing a mobile-first landing page that would drive user engagement, support community growth, and streamline the game creation process.
This case study outlines the research, design process, and outcomes achieved in collaboration with a multidisciplinary team.
As Senior Product Designer, I collaborated closely with engineering and creative leads to define a cohesive vision, establish design priorities, and ensure seamless cross-platform execution.
While online gaming communities are very popular, there was a noticeable gap in platforms that encouraged both social connection and creative collaboration among players.
Most existing platforms didn’t make it easy, fun, or rewarding to share your unique perspective of gaming.
FRVR set out to address this need by building a platform that validates users’ creativity and builds authentic community engagement.
Design a visually compelling, mobile-first landing page that attracts and retains both players and creators.
Lower the barrier for game creation by integrating intuitive AI-powered tools.
Build community engagement through interactive, collaborative features.
Enhance user retention and platform stickiness by making discovery and socialisation seamless and enjoyable.
To inform the design process, I conducted a competitive analysis of leading user-generated gaming platforms such as Roblox, Core, and Rec Room.
Additionally, I watched closely user interactions in relevant online forums and communities to understand collaborative behaviours.
This highlighted the importance of social validation, seamless co-creation, and the need for easy to use tools directly influencing our feature prioritisation and UX strategy.
I developed interactive prototypes and conducted usability tests with a targeted group of potential users, focusing on both newcomers and experienced creators.
Feedback emphasised the platform’s ease of use and the appeal of its social features, such as the Friends tab.
Based on this input, I iterated on the design introducing features like a game roulette to create moments of surprise making the whole experience more rewarding and interactive.

artSpydr is a global peer-to-peer marketplace designed to facilitate the buying, selling, and trading of original comic art while ensuring authenticity through blockchain technology. artSpydr merges the accessibility of eBay with the assurance of an auction house, offering a reliable platform for art enthusiasts worldwide.
As the product designer at artSpydr, I took care of market and user research, conducted user interviews, and crafted wireframes and prototypes.
Collaborating with a project manager, a CTO, and two React Native developers, I contributed to the design of the web and app interfaces, including a tracking system and bespoke branded packaging.
Noteworthy achievements include iterative design improvements driven by stakeholder input, securing funding, and addressing user pain points for enhanced engagement and satisfaction.
artSpydr addresses a gap in the market where collectors lack a cost-effective, end-to-end secure platform for transacting art.

Current challenges include exorbitant fees from auction houses, the insecurity of peer-to-peer marketplaces, time-consuming direct transactions, the absence of indisputable provenance, and a lack of reliable valuation methods.
The primary goal of artSpydr is to provide a uniquely convenient and secure platform for global art transactions.

The platform aims to match buyers and sellers efficiently, charging a fair commission, coordinating transactions, verifying art through a Machine Learning AI system, recording art on the Comic Art Blockchain for provenance, and offering additional services such as courier, insurance, and secure packaging.
I initiated the design journey by testing high-fidelity prototypes.
This strategic decision allowed me to uncover potential issues early on, refine design elements based on user feedback, and optimise the user interface for enhanced the usability.
Prioritising user-centricity, this phase served as a crucial foundation before diving into coding, mitigating risks, and aligning the design closely with user expectations.
A distinctive aspect of our design exploration involved testing the auction system with unique counter features using no-code platforms like Webflow.
By simulating a live auction environment, we got collector interest and participation levels without committing to full-scale development.
This approach not only provided valuable insights into user interactions but also enabled me to refine features based on real-world scenarios.
To address the growing importance of provenance, artSpydr employs The Comic Art Blockchain to encrypt, record, and tag art.
The aim is to initiate a historical process for provenance and chain of ownership in the original comic art market.
The solution I found was to design a robust proof of provenance tracking record that updates in real-time with every transaction.
Creating a system that seamlessly captures and reflects the chain of ownership for each piece of art sold on the platform required a careful balance between user transparency and data privacy.

artspydr.h: Logistics – Transit Insurance, Tracking, and Shipping
s: Ensuring an enriched transaction experience, artSpydr provides options for GPS-tracked transportation to local offices, bespoke courier services, transit insurance, and custom-designed packaging.
The UX solution was updating the booking screen for the courier service, introducing the option to use GPS trackers.
Given the constraints of tracker availability and cost-effectiveness, the design needed to provide a seamless booking experience while communicating limitations transparently.
I designed artSpydr's custom packaging incorporating a GPS tracker.
With an inner carton for protection and an outer triple-walled transit sleeve for the GPS tracker, the packaging process is streamlined, ensuring the safe delivery of verified artwork.
Beyond the technical considerations, the design challenge involved visually guiding users on how to employ the packaging effectively.
Ensuring the tracking process preserves the anonymity of both the seller and buyer, adding an extra layer of complexity.
artSpydr positioned itself as the intermediary expert in verifying artwork, a dedicated page was needed to keep both sellers and buyers informed about the status of the verification process.

UX solution was designing a visually intuitive interface that depicted the various stages of art verification while maintaining transparency and instilling confidence in users posed its own set of challenges.
Through the artSpydr project, we successfully created a secure, user-centric marketplace that addresses the pain points of collectors and artists alike.
The integration of innovative technologies such as blockchain and GPS tracking elevates the platform, making it a reliable and efficient solution for the global art community.
The emphasis on user experience and meticulous design choices positions artSpydr as a groundbreaking player in the comic art market.
Designed the app’s UI/UX, making smart microwave features intuitive and supporting healthier eating habits.
Today, convenience and health-conscious living are more important than ever.
With this in mind, I designed an application for a smart microwave that aims to not only simplify the microwave's functionality but also encourage healthier eating habits.
The goal of this project was to create an intuitive interface that seamlessly integrates with the user's grocery shopping and personal calendar, making meal planning and preparation more efficient.
As the lead UI/UX designer, I followed a structured and comprehensive design process.
Beginning with market research and competitor analysis, I explored industry trends, customer needs, and existing products to identify opportunities for improvement.
User research allowed me to gather critical insights into potential pain points and feature desires, which informed the subsequent feature prioritisation.
I developed sketches and wireframes to create initial visual representations and guide user flows, ensuring intuitive navigation.

Throughout, I analysed research outcomes and refined the app’s interface, culminating in high-fidelity designs that aligned with the project’s goals of improving usability and promoting healthier eating habits.

Before starting with any aspect of the design, it was crucial to comprehend the current usage patterns and needs of users in their home kitchens, particularly considering the increased reliance on home appliances due to changes in lifestyle and work conditions.
A key focus was understanding how home cooking habits have evolved, especially with more people spending time at home, either due to remote working or lifestyle changes.
This includes examining how users interact with their microwaves, and identifying potential gaps or frustrations in their current experiences.
The aim was to ensure that the app addresses these evolving needs effectively, enhancing convenience, efficiency, and enjoyment in home cooking.
In the User Research phase, I adopted a comprehensive approach to gain a deeper understanding of user needs and behaviours.
Initially, I engaged in conversations with potential users to gather firsthand insights.
These discussions were pivotal in revealing how individuals interact with their microwaves in their daily routines.

I delved into the specifics of their usage patterns, such as: Frequency of use Types of food they commonly prepare Overall satisfaction with the current functionalities I asked specific questions that aimed to identify one key function or feature they wished their microwave possessed but currently lacked.

This inquiry aimed to pinpoint innovative opportunities that could redefine the microwave user experience, focusing on practical improvements and enhancements that could bridge the gap between existing capabilities and user aspirations.
Limited Cooking Automation and Personalisation: Existing microwaves often lack advanced automation features for routine tasks and personalisation options.
Inadequate Integration with Smart Home Systems: Many current microwaves do not integrate seamlessly with smart home systems.
Lack of easy to use Interface and Accessibility: Current models frequently have non user-friendly interfaces or accessibility issues for users with visual impairments.
Insufficient Cooking Assistance and Guidance: Lack of cooking support, such as not having access to a variety of recipes, community suggestions.
Inefficiency in Cooking Automation: Lack of support for remote operations or cooking automation.
Users cannot start their microwave from a distance, like from their office, or set it to automatically prepare meals at a scheduled time.
Create and save custom cooking modes for favourite dishes.
The app can learn user habits, like making porridge every morning, and automate these tasks.
Store and quickly access favourite recipes.
Remotely turn on the microwave, including all settings.
Display current temperature and allow setting target temperatures.
Send alerts when cooking is complete or requires attention.
Suggest new recipes or when to use ingredients before they expire, integrated with the user's calendar.
Create and manage cooking routines and automate cooking.
Set and save presets for different family members.

A deep understanding of user needs is essential for user-centric design, highlighting significant opportunities for innovation in areas like automation, recipe integration, and smart home connectivity.

The critical importance of a user-friendly interface, as demonstrated by features such as the secure swipe gesture, is essential for seamlessly integrating a product like a microwave oven with a digital experience.
However, there are still a lot of inputs & features that could be added with proper testing and identifying the problem with the help of real-time user data.
